title: Researcher Citation Score
statement:
A researcher has written n papers. cites[i] is how many times paper i has been cited.

Their score is the largest number h such that at least h of their papers have at least h citations each. Return that score. A researcher whose papers are never cited scores 0.

examples.why: Three papers have ≥ 2 citations, so h = 2 works. Only two papers have ≥ 3, so h = 3 fails.
The score can never exceed the number of papers, however well cited they are.
One famous paper does not lift the score: you need two papers with ≥ 2 citations for h = 2.

hints: Try a candidate h and count the papers with at least h citations. Which values of h are even possible?
Sort the counts from high to low. Paper number i (1-based) in that order can support h = i only if it has at least i citations.
Without sorting: any count above n behaves exactly like n. Bucket the papers by min(cites, n), then walk h down from n keeping a running total of papers with at least h citations.

explain.intuition:
Sort the citation counts from highest to lowest. Going down the list, the i-th paper (1-based) is the i-th best, so "at least i papers with at least i citations" is true exactly when that paper has ≥ i citations. The score is the last position where this still holds.

The sort can be avoided. The score is at most n, so a paper with 5 000 citations counts the same as one with n. Put each paper in bucket min(cites, n). Then walk h from n down to 0, adding bucket h to a running count of papers with at least h citations. The first h where that count reaches h is the answer.
steps: Set atLeast = 0. For h from n down to 0: add bucket[h] to atLeast.
pitfalls: Returning a citation count instead of a paper count. With [9, 9, 9] the answer is 3, not 9.
Requiring exactly h papers instead of at least h.
Making the bucket array as large as the biggest citation count. Capping at n keeps it O(n).

solutions.title: Try every h
solutions.idea: For each h from n down to 0, count papers with at least h citations; return the first h that works.

solutions.title: Sort descending
solutions.idea: After sorting high to low, the answer is the number of leading positions i (1-based) whose paper has at least i citations.

solutions.title: Capped buckets
solutions.idea: Counts above n act like n. Bucket by min(c, n) and sweep h downward with a running count.

followups: The counts arrive already sorted in ascending order. Can you beat O(n)?
Papers keep arriving one at a time. How do you keep the score up to date cheaply?
